subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Gambler's Fallacy
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Gambler's Fallacy.

hook.text: The roulette ball landed on red six times straight. Gamblers piled onto black. Red hit again.

buildup.text: In 1913 at Monte Carlo, black came up 26 times in a row. Millions were lost betting on red.

discovery.text: The gambler's fallacy: believing past random events influence future ones. Each spin is independent.

twist.text: We see patterns in randomness because brains evolved to find structure, even where none exists.

climax.text: The coin has no memory. The roulette wheel has no memory. Past outcomes don't change future odds.

punchline.text: Randomness doesn't owe you a correction.

quiz.question: What is the gambler's fallacy?
options: Believing past random events affect future ones
Thinking you can always win if you try harder
Betting more money when you're losing

details.summary: The gambler's fallacy is the mistaken belief that past random outcomes influence future random outcomes. After several heads in a row, people expect tails to be due, even though each coin flip is independent and the coin has no memory.
details.whyItMatters: The gambler's fallacy drives poor decisions in gambling, investing, and any context involving random sequences. People see patterns in randomness and make bets based on imagined streaks and corrections that do not exist.
takeaways: Independent random events are not influenced by their predecessors
People expect random sequences to self-correct toward balance
The fallacy drives costly errors in gambling, investing, and risk assessment

faq.question: Why do people believe in hot streaks and corrections?
faq.answer: The human brain is a pattern-detection machine that finds patterns even in pure noise. The representativeness heuristic makes people expect small samples to mirror overall frequencies, so a run of heads feels like it must be followed by tails.

faq.question: Is the gambler's fallacy related to the hot hand belief?
faq.answer: They are mirror images. The gambler's fallacy expects reversal. The hot hand expects continuation. Both involve believing past random events predict future ones, but in opposite directions. Both are violations of independence.
